methods.label: Recognize medians through equal areas
methods.explanation:
Equal areas can identify a midpoint because triangles with a common altitude have areas proportional to their bases. Let the original triangle be \(ABC\), let \(X\) be the interior point, and write \([UVW]\) for the area of triangle \(UVW\). Extend \(AX\) to meet \(BC\) at \(D\).

Triangles \(ABX\) and \(ACX\) share base \(AX\). Their areas are equal exactly when the perpendicular distances from \(B\) and \(C\) to line \(AX\) are equal. Since \(AD\) lies on that same line, this is also exactly the condition that triangles \(ABD\) and \(ACD\) have equal areas.

The latter pair have a common altitude from \(A\) to \(BC\). Their areas are therefore equal exactly when \(BD=DC\), meaning that \(AD\) is a median. We have proved
\[
[ABX]=[ACX]
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
X\text{ lies on the median from }A.
\]
If all three small triangles have equal areas, applying this argument at each vertex shows that \(X\) lies on all three medians. This proves necessity.

Conversely, if \(X\) is the intersection of the medians, the equivalence at \(A\) gives \([ABX]=[ACX]\), and the equivalence at \(B\) gives \([ABX]=[BCX]\). Thus all three areas are equal, proving sufficiency. The answer is E.
